description:
Microsoft has discovered a new piece of malware that not only spies on data but also renders entire systems unusable. The malware, known as GigaWiper, combines several destructive functions with a powerful backdoor for attackers.

Security researchers at Microsoft Threat Intelligence first detected the activity back in October 2025. The recently published analysis reveals the full extent of the malware’s capabilities.

According to the report, GigaWiper isn’t a traditional wiper malware with a single purpose—it’s far worse. Other security researchers are also tracking the malware under the name BlueRabbit.
title: Microsoft found malware that destroys PCs. Here’s who’s actually at risk

title: Got Windows 10 ESU? Microsoft sent you an email you might’ve missed

description:
Scareware websites are designed to frighten people into taking actions they wouldn’t otherwise take, like installing malicious software or calling fake technical support. To help protect against these scams, Microsoft Edge includes a scareware blocker, although it may need to be enabled first.

Typical examples of scareware include pages that suddenly open in full-screen mode, display false virus warnings, or claim your computer has dangerous security vulnerabilities. Often, loud alarm sounds play or simulated system messages appear.

The goal behind scareware is to trick users into downloading protective software (which is actually malware) or granting remote access to their computer to someone posing as a technical support expert. Edge’s scareware blocker uses AI to identify these fake websites and warn users before they interact with th
title: Turn on Microsoft Edge’s scareware blocker before you need it

description:
Microsoft has begun testing a new “PC Insights” feature in Copilot for Windows 11 that helps users analyze their computer’s performance and answer questions about the system’s status, reports Windows Latest.

With the user’s permission, Copilot can now analyze CPU and memory usage, available storage space, graphics card details, connected USB devices, network status, battery health, and BIOS version.

The idea is that users will be able to ask direct questions about their hardware, to which Copilot can respond based on the computer’s actual current status. However, PC Insights can only read and analyze information—it can’t automatically resolve issues for you.

title: Ask Copilot why your PC is slow. It might actually have a real answer

description:
Many gaming PCs aren’t delivering their full potential because the monitor and graphics card are connected via HDMI. While this usually works without any problems, it does not always make full use of the system’s capabilities, particularly when using high refresh rates, variable refresh rates, and modern graphics cards.

DisplayPort is designed for PC use, offering a more stable and less error-prone connection. Anyone wishing to connect their monitor correctly should check whether a switch is advisable and how to implement it correctly. The most important difference lies in the technical orientation of the standards.

title: Why DisplayPort beats HDMI for gaming PCs

description:
Cybersecurity advice is sometimes extremely straightforward. Your password leaked? Change it. Your PC needs updates? Apply them. You want to install pirated software? Don’t.

But more often, cybersecurity advice is a simplification of complex details—and results in opposite instructions from various experts. That’s confusing for many people, and I don’t blame anyone for feeling that way.

One recent example: I tend to recommend that people use a guest Wi-Fi network at home. But a colleague pointed out that Mike Danseglio, a certified ethical hacker and periodic contributor to PCWorld, had told him not to use one. So who was he supposed to believe?
title: Stop looking for ironclad cybersecurity answers. They often don’t exist

description:
We’ve all been in a spot where we wish we had the technical know-how to fix a cracked phone screen, deal with a laptop that won’t charge, or bring an old game console back to life. I’ve been in these exact situations and instead of needlessly tossing my electronics and buying new ones, I first turn to iFixit. It’s the best place on the web to learn how to repair your own electronics.

The site has thousands of free step-by-step repair guides covering everything from smartphones and laptops to cameras, game consoles, kitchen appliances, and even some vehicles. Each guide includes a plethora of helpful photos, a list of the tools you’ll need, and repair difficulty ratings so you know what you’re getting into before you pick up a screwdriver.
title: This is the first site I visit when my tech breaks
